subject: maths
title: Pythagoras Foundations
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the most famous rule in maths — a² + b² = c² — and use it to find the hypotenuse.
meta_desc: GCSE Maths Pythagoras' Theorem foundations — the rule a²+b²=c², recognising the hypotenuse, and famous Pythagorean triples.
final_note: You can state Pythagoras' theorem, spot the hypotenuse and find it for whole-number triples like 3-4-5.

concepts.def: In a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c².
Longest side, opposite the right angle.
The two sides that meet at the right angle.
Whole numbers a, b, c with a² + b² = c².

walkthroughs.body_html:
Pythagoras' theorem says: in any right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c².

Here a and b are the two short sides (the ones touching the 90° corner) and c is the hypotenuse — the longest side, opposite the right angle.

It only works for right-angled triangles. No 90°? No Pythagoras.

Before you start any Pythagoras question, find the hypotenuse:

• It's the longest side.
• It's opposite the right angle (it never touches it).
• It's always called c in the formula.

The other two sides are a and b. It doesn't matter which is which — addition is commutative (a² + b² = b² + a²).

Example: right-angled triangle, short sides 3 and 4. Find c.

c² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = √25 = 5.

This is the famous 3-4-5 triangle.

Worth memorising (Pythagorean triples):

• 3, 4, 5 → 9 + 16 = 25
• 5, 12, 13 → 25 + 144 = 169
• 8, 15, 17 → 64 + 225 = 289

Spot one in a question and the answer pops out without a calculator.
